analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent business tax breaks for equipment purchases and research, doubles the research credit, and creates new credits for domestic drug manufacturing.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on October 9, 2020, received no committee action or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut federal taxes for businesses in several ways: make permanent the rule letting companies deduct the full cost of equipment in one year instead of over time; let companies deduct research costs immediately; double the research tax credit from 20% to 40%; create new tax credits of 10.5% of income for companies making drugs and medical supplies in the U.S. and 30% for advanced medical manufacturing equipment; let multinational corporations move intangible property like patents back to the U.S. without owing tax on the gain; and expand deductions for start-up costs. The bill contains no offsetting tax increases, so the cost would be added to the federal deficit. It never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that buy equipment and spend heavily on research would pay less federal tax, and the biggest research spenders — large technology and pharmaceutical firms — would gain the most from a doubled research credit. Pharmaceutical and medical device makers would get new credits for producing in the U.S., and multinationals could bring foreign-held patents and other intangibles home without recognizing taxable gain. Small start-ups would get a larger up-front deduction for start-up costs and easier access to research credits.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent 100% expensing for business equipment, software, and certain other property, letting companies deduct the full cost in the year purchased instead of over many years [S2][S3].
Doubles the research and development tax credit rate from 20% to 40% and lets small businesses claim up to $500,000 of the credit against payroll taxes, twice the current limit [S2][S3].

Creates a 10.5% credit on income from manufacturing active pharmaceutical ingredients and medical countermeasures in the U.S., plus a 30% credit for advanced medical manufacturing equipment placed in service before 2028 [S3].

Lets a controlled foreign corporation distribute patents, software, and other intangible property to U.S. shareholders without recognizing gain, so the return of foreign-held intellectual property carries no tax [S3].

Raises the immediate deduction for start-up and organizational costs to $20,000 (with a phase-down starting at $120,000) and preserves start-up losses and credits when the company is later acquired [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — and ultimately taxpayers — would bear the cost. The bill contains no offsetting revenue increases, so the cost of these business tax cuts would be added to the deficit. Supporters argue the benefits reach workers through faster growth and higher wages, but the direct beneficiaries are the businesses that reduce their tax bills.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offsets, so all of its tax cuts would be added to the federal deficit rather than paid for [S3].

The largest dollar benefits flow to the biggest taxpaying entities: profitable corporations with large equipment or research budgets, and drug manufacturers that would collect a new 10.5% credit on manufacturing income, while households receive nothing directly [S2][S3].

The provision letting multinationals move foreign-held intangible property back to U.S. owners without recognizing gain gives companies a tax-free step-up on assets that were shifted abroad in the first place [S3].
Benefits to workers depend on companies choosing to invest the savings in expansion and hiring rather than shareholder returns; the bill attaches no such condition [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters frame the package as a growth plan: faster write-offs and a bigger research credit should encourage investment, and the medical manufacturing credits respond to the pandemic-era shortage of drugs and supplies made abroad. The counterweight is that every provision is unpaid-for deficit spending targeted at businesses, the largest benefits accrue to the biggest corporations, and the intangible-property provision lets multinationals avoid tax on assets returning home. Whether the growth benefits would reach ordinary workers is an indirect and contested proposition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died automatically when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Brady introduced the bill on October 9, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
Fifteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much either way. The corporations, drug manufacturers, and multinationals that would have received the tax breaks got nothing, and taxpayers were spared the deficit cost of an unpaid-for business tax cut package.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; intended corporate beneficiaries gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
for.role: Sponsor; senior Republican on the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 9, 2020, laying out the Republican business-tax package of permanent expensing, a doubled research credit, and new medical manufacturing credits.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup; the bill received no action after its referral and expired at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship was Republican — the sponsor and 15 cosponsors were House Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors — and the bill never reached a vote in the Democratic-controlled committee or chamber.

industries.note: A doubled research credit and immediate expensing of research costs would sharply cut the tax bills of the largest research spenders, at a cost to federal revenue with no direct benefit to households.

New credits — 10.5% of income from domestic drug-ingredient manufacturing and 30% for advanced manufacturing equipment — would subsidize production of medicines and medical countermeasures in the U.S. That could improve supply security that pandemic shortages exposed, but it channels public money to drugmakers' profits.
A new rule would let foreign subsidiaries distribute patents, software, and know-how to U.S. owners without recognizing taxable gain, letting companies bring appreciated intangibles home tax-free.

A larger up-front start-up deduction, doubled payroll-tax offset for research credits, and preserved start-up losses after an acquisition would lower the cost of launching and scaling a small business.
